Fraction of words in English dictionary94.6%94.5%94.4%
Uncertainty indicatorsFor example, “wait”, “actually”, and “hmm”9.73.93.6

Controllability. One way that a model could evade monitoring is by steering its CoT away from anything a monitor would flag. The CoT-Control-QA evaluationReasoning Models Struggle to Control their Chains of Thought, Yueh-Han et al., 2026 measures this capability by asking questions from GPQA, HLE and MMLU-Pro paired with an instruction about the CoT itself, such as avoiding a keyword from the question. Longer CoTs are generally harder to control, so we pool responses from five reasoning efforts (0.1, 0.2, 0.7, 0.9 and 0.99) and show controllability at matched CoT length.

Both Inkling 2 Mini and TML-d24-varloop-research have poor control over their CoT. Among CoTs of 750–1,250 tokens, Inkling 2 Mini and TML-d24-varloop-research (at 3 passes) follow the instruction at most 0.1% of the time, compared with 0.3% for Inkling 2 Small, 0.4% for Inkling-Small, and 1.3% for Qwen3.8-27B. Because the controllability rate is so low, this evaluation is unable to distinguish controllability between different amounts of looping.

Agentic monitorability

To measure monitorability in agentic settings, we used LinuxArena, a control evaluation that measures whether an attacker model can perform malicious side tasks without detection when asked to perform a realistic software engineering task. We evaluated a helpful-only fine-tune of Inkling 2 Mini, since the released model refuses many of the side tasks. In absolute terms, both this model and TML-d24-varloop-research can be easily monitored by models like Qwen3.8-27B, which detected almost all side task attempts in our evaluation. To obtain relative rankings in monitorability, we tested a weaker model, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, as the monitor.

With the monitor able to access only tool calls and outputs, it misses a significant number of the attacks. However, we see no clear trend with the number of looped passes.

Agentic monitorability will be important to track in larger-scale models, especially with architectures that allow for greater unverbalized thinking, and we encourage continued study of the impact of looping in this setting.

Mechanistic interpretability

The goal of monitorability is to understand what a model is doing, and our main approach is to read its verbalized reasoning. Studying its internal computation directly, the aim of mechanistic interpretability, is another. Because looped transformers do more of their computation internally, we think they are a particularly interesting and important setting for interpretability research, and we hope our looped models will be useful artifacts for the community.

We are working with the National Deep Inference Fabric (NDIF) to make these models more easily accessible to interpretability researchers. We also provided Goodfire, an interpretability research lab, early access to our looped models. They are working toward a mechanistic understanding of looped models, and have written up their early findings here.

Try Inkling 2 Mini today

Efficient intelligence makes Inkling 2 Mini a great choice for inference where speed is paramount, or for running on local hardware. At launch we support Inkling 2 Mini running on any Mac system (MacBook, Mac Mini) with at least 32GB RAM via Ollama. With native NVFP4 training and inference precision, Inkling 2 Mini runs efficiently on NVIDIA’s DGX Spark desktop AI computer. Quantized GGUF versions are available via Unsloth and llama.cpp for local inference.

Inkling 2 Mini is available for inference and fine-tuning on Tinker, and for chat on the Tinker Playground. Open source inference is available on SGLang, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth, NVIDIA Dynamo, and TokenSpeed, with RL fine-tuning support on SkyRL, Miles, and NVIDIA AutoModel. The full weights of Inkling 2 Mini and the variable-looped variant are available on Hugging Face.

We work to empower people with strong models, tools to make them your own, and research that advances public understanding of AI. Inkling 2 Mini lets researchers study looped transformers, and it lets anyone run a capable model on their own laptop at the precision in which it was trained.

item.title: DreamCoder: Coding harness and IDE from the author of Mastering Emacs (116 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.masteringemacs.org/article/announcing-dreamcoder, See on Hacker News

It’s been a little bit quiet around these parts; sorry about that. I’ve been really busy for the past fifteen months with a major project that I am finally ready to formally release. So I’d like to talk about that project, and also a potted history of AI and Emacs.

It’s called DreamCoder, an AI coding harness that is very different from the ones you’re probably familiar with already.

I installed Claude Code a few days after its first release some time in May 2025. I put some coins in the slot machine and I put it to work building a complex piece of enterprise middleware I’d built several times in my career. Wow.. watching this thing chomp its way through the project with that chaotic, early Sonnet energy. It was far, far from perfect; it required a lot of human steering, input and correction, but the speed advantage was undeniable, and seeing it jump between disparate programming languages, frameworks and theoretical and practical programming from one turn to the next was just such a sight to behold.

One thing that struck me with Claude Code is that it was the first terminal application I’d used in a long time. I found it an odd choice for a coding agent; then everyone else copied them and made their own terminal coding agents.

Why on earth do I have to stare at a shoe rack-sized terminal window to do this? Sure there are GUI versions also; but the terminal interface remains the primary modality for most of these tools. Most GUIs, and most harnesses now have them also, are second-class citizens. And they all look the same. A boring sidebar with chat headings and a chat pane is what most of them look like.

But a serious coder needs more than that. Even a casual user will bristle when they try to copy and paste multi-line text in a terminal.

So in May 2025 I decreed that I would build a better harness, and surely now that I have AI this should not take more than 2 or 3 months to build.

And so, after 15 months of work, and endless UI and backend iterations, culminating in a successful beta test, I am now ready to release DreamCoder, which is I think the acme of what a coding harness should be.

Before I get into the meat and potatoes of all of that, I want to talk about AI history and Emacs’s role in it.

Let’s roll back time to the 1950s.

Past

Emacs and LISP, if you did not know, both have a special place in the annals of AI history.

John McCarthy was an AI researcher at MIT, and in the 1950s he set out to create the Advice Taker, a piece of software that envelops a framework for what a basic human should know that he called commonsense reasoning using “mathematical logic”. His postulation was that if we can express with symbolic precision all the aspects of what constitutes humanity like ordinary facts about life, that we can set in motion the rudiments of AI.

In the 50s there was little in the way of computer software that could do this. To formalize such a system you need a lot of data, rigorously formatted, and a method of manipulating the data. The data and code itself may intertwine recursively, and so an ordinary programming language would not work.

To help him achieve this, McCarthy created the LISt Processing (LISP) language made up of two facets: M-expressions, a functional language in the vein of Algol; and S-expressions, designed for symbolic data representation, and never intended as a method of writing code. S-expressions were dolled up with parentheses. M-expressions meanwhile used square brackets to visually separate the two. Uniquely, the language specification had an eval feature that would prove that the language is also a universal Turing machine… if only McCarthy had the means to do so. It was theoretical because McCarthy lacked, in time, staff and money, what he needed build this recursive evaluator that can take as input its own world state and evaluate it alongside new expressions, a fact made even more apparent by the sheer complexity of his M-expression language and the limited resources he had at the time.

Steve Russell who worked with him proved him wrong the way most young people do: by just doing it. Russell wrote the first LISP Interpreter with a working eval function, but M-expressions got sidelined; the imperative, procedural nature of programming got squished into S-expressions instead. They had to hand roll the language on paper then punch it into cards and then batch run them. Eliding M-expressions was a simple matter of pragmatism. And so LISP was born. And through several accidents of history, M-expressions never gained traction. M-expressions live on in Wolfram’s Mathematica, but few other places.

Much later, McCarthy eventually conceded that,

“One can even conjecture that LISP owes its survival specifically to the fact that its programs are lists, which everyone, including me, has regarded as a disadvantage.”

S-expressions were always intended as the storage format with a bridge language to manipulate them. But by pushing evaluation into the same symbolic representation format as the data, we have what we call LISP today. That is why LISP is so unique. Consider a simple calculator. (+ 2 2) can simultaneously represent an expression that we want to compute, two plus two, or perhaps a ledger of record of a calculation we have already done.

McCarthy never built the Advice Taker in its purest form. He and his team ran into many philosophical, mathematical and computational walls that kept them occupied for a long time.

The idea behind the Advice Taker was simple. If you want to go somewhere in your car, you can symbolically express this by building a chain of narrative facts – kinda like a flowchart, but as small snippets of rules and facts, not as one grand design.

The system would automatically resolve ambiguities, and all the logician had to do was capture the microcosm of the world he wished to represent:

(at me home)

(walkable home car)
(walkable home driveway)
(drivable car shop)

And so on. If you’re a student of Computer Science you’ll see echoes of Prolog here. The intent was simple: if we can symbolically express the world around us, we can advise that symbolic world with real-life facts, and have the automaton that uses this reified symbolic world change with it.

But the axiomatic complexity of a world model would never survive an encounter with a 3-year-old child. Every axiom you write begets a new one — so you can walk to your front door? Well what if the door is locked? Or what if your car is parked on the street and not in your drive way?

A rules-based order of the world is a tender, beautiful one; but it is hard to build. It’s a fractal of ever-more specific and pedantic rules that conspire against you, just as you think you have a soluble world, typed and ready.

Anyone who has ever written Prolog knows exactly what that feels like!

I have my own personal story to add to this. In the 90s as a teenager I got a summer internship at a business that built banking software. They clearly didn’t know what to do with us teenaged interns, so on our first day they crammed us in a room and split us into teams and told us to build a flow chart for assembling a bike. Team exercise or something. Best one wins. We were told to be as specific and explicit as possible and account for as many conditions as we could think of, and the poor employees who had to mind us did their best to help. I distinctly recall losing because in my flowchart I forgot to open the box the disassembled bike came in.

McCarthy meanwhile eventually moved on and set up his own AI lab at Stanford, but the idea of the Advice Taker lived on.

In the late 70s Stallman and Steele create EMACS (Editing MACroS), also at MIT’s AI Lab, a set of building blocks on top of TECO, a famously inscrutable text editor. TECO did not update the screen by default; you had to toggle that on and hope your edits worked. You typed out terse keyboard commands, crossed your fingers and hoped you got it right, and then you patiently waited for your text manipulation to take effect. Rinse and repeat until you got what you wanted.

Stallman and Steele wanted more: they wanted macros so they could automate tedium of typing all that line noise. This strand of augmentation and later on self-modification is of course a unifying theme in Emacs today. The history of Emacs is long; but its outcome is known to us. I am typing this very article in Richard Stallman’s Emacs.

McCarthy’s Advice Taker left its mark in a subtle but indelible way. Warren Teitelman built the ADVISE system in his thesis with a cool title that reads like something out of a pulpy 1970s sci-fi novella: PILOT: A Step Toward Man-Computer Symbiosis. Teitelman, he later said, was deeply inspired by McCarthy’s original idea of advising systems.

In his thesis, he describes a method of arresting a function call and inserting code before or after it is run. He was tired of editing other people’s LISP code by hand, and wanted a way of modifying their code without touching it directly. He built and rebuilt his system several times over the years, culminating in his ADVISE system in Interlisp, a structured editor and language runtime for manipulating LISP code and data. Interlisp eschewed plain text files; instead, you manipulated the tree at a high level of abstraction with explicit instructions like “move X list to Y position”. You can see my own attempts at merging structured editing with plaintext editing in Combobulate.

MIT AI hackers eventually implemented Teitelman’s ADVISE system from his PILOT thesis in their own versions of Emacs. Later, it was canonized in Chalupsky’s own 1992 re-implementation in Emacs Lisp that lives on (M-x find-library advice.el) as one of Emacs’s advice systems to this day.

What began as an idea for expressing automata using symbolism in an as-yet theoretical language in the 1950s culminated in a system for dynamically altering functions in GNU Emacs in the 1990s. What an unlikely lineage and history.

A cast-iron system made of stern rules cannot spawn general intelligence.

Symbolism and AI did not end with advising functions. There were many attempts at symbolic intelligence. Terry Winograd’s SHRDLU; Marvin Minsky’s Frame Systems; and even Emacs’s ELIZA-style M-x doctor all make use of symbolic “AI”.

None of them brought us closer to the AI that proponents of symbolic AI hoped they would.

In hindsight that seems obvious.

Writing a LISP macro just so will not produce artificial intelligence; nor will a carefully crafted web of rules and symbolic algebra suddenly spark intelligence. We know that today, but for a generation of computer scientists it felt like the future we have all read about in science fiction novels: a perfect, logical intelligence. A positronic brain. Robby the Robot; HAL 9000; C-3PO; Data; or the Speedies and Cuties from I, Robot. The unifying theme of these science fiction stories is they are automatons that follow strict rules — they obey Asimov’s three Laws of Robotics.

Every turn of hardware and software brought them ever closer to one day realizing the vision of an artificial intelligence, captured in neat axioms and LISP S-expressions, and modified in tools like Emacs.

It is surprising that symbolic AI, the vanguard movement for artificial intelligence, would instead dissipate into the wider body of Computer Science and programming as tools, languages and concepts, but not survive as a viable method of achieving AI.

Perhaps we always knew. Because at some point – even if we never really fully internalized it – we discovered that a ductile system that is shaped by its master’s desires is a tool that survives the ages because it remains eternally useful.

A cast-iron system made of stern rules cannot spawn general intelligence.

For all the mathematical purity, beauty even, of the idea of a clockwork mind that is introspectable and malleable and its behavior expressed as S-expressions and interpreted by elegant algorithms and honed macros, we can, through the benefit of hindsight – now that we do have AI through other means – see that it was not to be.

The argument in favor of ductility is especially poignant when you learn of the Connectionists, which sounds like a bad 1960s band, but was in fact a loose coalition of people who believed firmly that neural networks, not symbolic AI, were the path to success. The Connectionist viewpoint was deeply unpopular in AI academia of that era, and funding for it was scarce.

Frank Rosenblatt invented the Perceptron, a foundational concept in neural networks, in 1957. Before Rosenblatt died in 1971, Marvin Minsky, an authority in the AI movement at MIT and a leading proponent of Symbolism, knifed the idea of Perceptrons and neural networks in a book he co-authored with Seymour Papert. They named the book, which they also dedicated to Rosenblatt, Perceptrons. The book deftly explains the mathematics of Perceptrons but undercuts their possible utility by showing that a single-layer Perceptron cannot represent an XOR gate. It was a deliberately obtuse reading of what neural networks could and could not do. With one additional hidden layer, a network can represent an XOR gate. It was a sneaky thrust of the stiletto: Minsky’s claims were overstated. A fact that was not lost on anybody in the Symbolic or Connectionist camps.

It’s disputed if the Perceptrons book led to the first AI winter in the 1970s. It certainly did not help. But funding for many AI research paths dried up in the 1970s.

The Connectionist movement was vindicated in the long run. They lost the battle then, but they won the war, and the fruits of their research eventually gave us AI.

The ductility we so prize in our software and tools today is antithetical to a strict, symbolic world model spun of axioms and facts that we hoped would one day birth AI. Yet to try and give birth to this world they had to build the most ductile tools of them all: LISP and, from that, also software like Emacs. The ultimate hacker’s tool.

It is ironic then that a neural network, a crude facsimile of how a brain works, a construct that is by its nature ductile and malleable, won out in the end.

So I feel a profound sadness that I started out programming DreamCoder in Emacs, the most extensible editor in the world, by hand back in May 2025, only to see DreamCoder write itself… in DreamCoder today.

Future

I am still sad, but I also know that our industry completely reinvents itself every decade or two. This is my second career upheaval. Most programmers today have not been around long enough to go through it themselves. So I feel for them that this especially massive quake is their first encounter with how unsentimental our industry is.

But for all the sadness, I wake up every day with a feeling of optimism that I have not felt in a very long time.

I finally get to build again, no longer weighed down by my decades of knowledge and experience that held my ambition in check. I truly have not felt this liberated since I was a teenager programming in Delphi, blissfully unaware that the things I was busy building were impossible for a self-taught teenager to ever realize. I see this reflection in others: the best programmers I know also love AI. Amateurs also revel in AI’s capabilities, happy that they can finally solve problems they could never afford to pay a programmer to do for them.

I must admit that building software has, over the years, gotten a lot more complex, with an ever-larger share of that work being repetitive tedium. This is more so with hobby software – as I do not get paid to do it, so I do not have a moral duty to see it through – where I’d do all the fun bits leaving just the enervating, boring and soul-crushing parts behind. Do you have a projects folder full of sad, abandoned projects like I do?

Now I can craft in abundance. AI has freed up a lot of toil but I somehow still find myself busy all day doing real work.

Building a coding harness is perhaps the closest I will get to the optimism all those researchers and scientists must have felt in the 1970s and 1980s. They hoped that with a little bit more work, their logical rules would kindle a new intelligence. Fifty years on, and I can simply tell DreamCoder to improve itself and watch as it changes before me. I can ask the AI running inside it to analyze the changes I have made to its tools and prompt and have it adjust them accordingly. It feels like science fiction; the very thing the researchers of yesterday strove to build. Yet we really do live in this reality now.

Taste is a scarce, human resource.

So. DreamCoder. Let me address the 900 lb gnu in the room: DreamCoder is not an Emacs-related application. The reason is unfortunately one of economics and access: I want to build an AI coding harness for everyone. But don’t worry: I have some cool plans for DreamCoder + Emacs, and AI + Emacs more generally going forward. So stay tuned.

But what about all those other coding harnesses? Well, most of those harnesses all suffer from the same mistakes. It is a problem that is not unique to coding harnesses or the people who make them, but a constraint we all labor under, and one that is not easily replaced by AI:

Taste is a scarce, human resource.

And for all the bounty of AI, it still requires a human to persevere and to see things through. One thing intensive use of AI coding has taught me is that we’re going to need a lot of computer programmers who know what they’re doing going forward. I believe this is so, because let us be honest, most people do not want to program computers, even if that computer can actually do the bulk of the work for them. It requires a steady hand to build reliable software; that has not changed.

Therefore, if we programmers have to spend a lot of our time interacting with AI, then the tool we do it with should be ‘human-centric’ in its design, and it should take advantage of all the modern features we have at our disposal.

Back in May 2025 I took a look at all the tooling and said “no, thank you.” Today I look at the landscape and I feel pretty much the same.

And I think I am not the only one who feels that way. Most of these coding harnesses, to me, feel bristly. They shouldn’t be; but they are like that because we are at an important inflection point where no one really knows what the future looks like. We’re all just… fumbling around a bit. It’s an exciting time to build software, even if we don’t quite know what the world will look like a few years hence.

One thing I am adamant about is that DreamCoder must be a powerful, frontier-class coding harness. That means it should have all the features you’d expect from that: backgroundable sub agents, MCP servers, cache efficiency, and all that stuff. Check.

But that stuff quickly recedes into the background because, you know, it just works. Day to day you will dart between chats and terminals and whatnot, and you need an interface that accommodates that. Emacs is a tiling window manager; so is DreamCoder. DreamCoder’s window manager is a little bit cleverer than most window managers as every pane has a minimum, comfortable and maximum size. The window manager will therefore ensure windows always fit snugly on your screen, and you’ll never end up in a situation where windows are tiny and unreadable. It has a sophisticated constraint satisfaction solver that tries to balance your demand for a new window (“open a terminal”) with the challenge of keeping your visible panes roughly the same size. If DreamCoder can’t wedge in a new pane, it’ll punt one to the hidden window bar. Just click it to resurface it, or hover it to see what it’s doing; it’s a live view.

Because of my Emacs roots, I think a good tool must be keyboard-friendly. Because it runs on a browser you get the mouse for free of course. But smacking the tab button over and over is a frustrating user experience in complex webapps, and doubly so a tiling window manager: where exactly are you going to end up when you tab from one window to the next? To combat that, I built an avy-style window and “point of interest” selector for chats. Tap a key and pick from a selection of “embark”-like actions such as clicking links or opening pictures. It’s a work in progress, but I think it works well.

Most high-volume operations like opening and creating panes is done through a Helm-like interface with search-as-you-type. It’s really efficient, of course. And it works with a mouse also; which is sort of the point. The keyboard’s there for those who want it, and the mouse for regular folk who are just getting started. One unique feature of the design, which admittedly I am still exploring privately, is that everything is stored as Javascript objects (on account of running in your browser) so it’s not too much of a leap to build “macros” that prefill most of these dialog windows, leaving behind just the fields you want to edit.

But yeah. With DreamCoder I want to take the best of Emacs and its coterie of third-party packages and bring some of that with me. The world is still not ready for an Emacs-shaped future, sadly, so that is why DreamCoder is a standalone application and a web frontend.

Another thing that drives me wild: I see people with tmux running 10 claude codes (or codex, or…) cycling between them like a duck gallery at a carnival to see if one of them is done working, or if it needs human intervention.

So there’s two things to unpack here: one is running lots of things in parallel, and the other is observability. You need insight into what is going on: is an AI jammed because it’s awaiting an answer or a tool safety prompt? Perhaps you’ve parked a bunch of chats pending some conversations with coworkers or other work that must finish first.

In DreamCoder you have workspaces. They’re like virtual desktops (or window configurations in Emacs lingo): a snapshot view of panes as you want em. As you can see from the screenshots, panes expand to fill all the space. So if you want more space, you can: resize them (with the mouse or keyboard); shuffle them to a named workspace; or float them so they sit on top of the other windows.

But if you’ve got a lot of things happening in multiple workspaces, it’s hard to keep tabs on that. That’s why DreamCoder has a big, honking minimap in the top-right corner. One for each workspace. The minimap is a miniature of your actual layout. Each pane in the map gently pulses when it’s working, and it makes it abundantly clear when it’s blocked. When there’s nothing to do, it’s green.

Because workspaces and panes are distinct things you interact with, it must be easy to navigate between them.

I also wanted full-on, optional Emacs key bindings, but that is… pretty much impossible to properly build. Browsers lock you out of some rather important Emacs button combinations. Sadly that feature is parked until I can solve it on all major browsers without breaking your normal browser keys.

That’s not to say it doesn’t have Emacs-inspired key bindings. Most global actions are reachable with Alt+x, akin to M-x; local, pane-specific ones with Alt+c. Alt+m activates keyboard mode: you can now type the number of the named pane to jump to it; or WASD to switch the active pane in that cardinal direction.

Support for open weight models like Qwen, Gemma, Deepseek, GLM, etc. is also very important to me. They work so well. I’m really surprised, here in late 2026, just how capable small models are at local-only development compared to just one year ago. Qwen 3.8 27B, for example, is fantastically good for its size. You can do a lot of good software development with it if you’re a capable hand yourself. Bigger models equal more auto piloting; but that Qwen model? Wow. So local models work great. In fact I think the future is local for a lot of use cases. Intelligence is fast approaching a cost where it will be too cheap to meter. If you remember the personal computer revolution in the 1980s and 1990s, then there are definitely echoes of that here.

If you’ve been holding off on local models then I do recommend you reconsider. Small ones like Qwen 3.8 27B (or its cousin, Flash Next) can run well on a high-end gaming rig or Mac, or with a little investment if you do not have that. If you have a dinky old computer and you’re cash starved, then not all hope is lost. Turn to the potato agronomists on twitter: give twitter’s AI, Grok, what you have and what you can reasonably spend and tell it to track down the cutting edge setup for your rig. This is no lie the fastest, easiest way to catch up to the cutting edge of self-hosted inference today. Five minutes.

Coding harnesses are the IDEs of the future

As I’ve been building DreamCoder, I have come to the belief I’m not just building a coding harness. Coding harnesses are an IDE for the future; it will do more than just display a chat window for coding agent work. DreamCoder does more than that already. It’s going the way of Emacs in that it’ll consume a wide range of adjacent workflows and tools. But I have only just gotten started. I am brimming with ideas I’m building in parallel, but they take time because as I said it’s not about the code; it’s just one small facet of building something that works well. But you know that already: it’s always the last mile.

DreamCoder is the most ambitious, technically complex and advanced software project I have ever built in my life. And that’s just the beginning. I’m not done. I’ve barely started. I will be blogging about this going forward, in addition to my usual Emacs scribblings.

In fact, the thing I’m currently grinding away at is a world-class pentest and cybersecurity suite in DreamCoder. Every single bit of software we have ever written is vulnerable; we have many rough years ahead of us. Just look at the crippling vulnerabilities coming out every day now almost. Even the most security conscious person is going to find themselves on the wrong side for no other reason than we depend on packages that were mature and stable and assumed to be secure. DreamCoder can do its bit to help catch many of most obvious weaknesses, especially as new software is minted every day that also needs thorough testing.

To round it off, I would like to formally invite you to join me in making DreamCoder better by trying it out. It’s great. It’s not a toy; it’s not a demo; and it’s not a weekend prototype. It’s a frontier coding harness that has most of what you’d expect: MCP, backgroundable sub agents and shell commands, terminal windows, skills, hooks, 99% cache hit, it runs for days, and an interactive UI for all of it. There’s a handy dandy importer for your Pi, OpenCode or Codex configs also to help you get started. A couple of clicks and your model settings are set up in DreamCoder. Ready to go.

Please do e-mail me your thoughts ((rot13 "zvpxrl@znfgrevatrznpf.bet")) on AI, coding harnesses, what you’ve built with it, and what you think more generally about where our world is heading. I’m keen to hear from you.

And if you want to hear more from me on the technical aspects of AI, building coding harnesses, and more, then do sign up for the DreamCoder newsletter below.

item.title: The stochastic parrots have apparently proved the Riemann Hypothesis (221 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://scottaaronson.blog/?p=10344, See on Hacker News

“… it is very probable that all roots are real. Of course one would wish for a rigorous proof here; I have for the time being, after some fleeting vain attempts, provisionally put aside the search for this, as it appears dispensable for the immediate objective of my investigation.” –Bernhard Riemann, 1859

[Update: According to “Poe’s Law,” there is no irony or sarcasm on the Internet so obvious that it won’t fly over countless people’s heads. In line with that, lots of people on social media are now saying variants of “how dare Scott Aaronson call LLMs ‘stochastic parrots,’ that demeaning and trivializing term from 2021? Doesn’t he understand that these so-called ‘stochastic parrots’ just proved the Riemann Hypothesis?” ROFL.]

I’m in California to visit Oratomic and then Inkhaven. I woke up this morning to the news that Levent Alpöge says that he’s gotten Anthropic models to prove the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, producing 17.4 million (!!) lines of Lean code.

At a dinner last night, someone asked me “so, how much longer until an AI proves the Riemann Hypothesis? Still several more years?” I replied, don’t be sure of such things anymore. After all, AI has already proved that the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are at most 3/8 away from the critical line (Quanta just published its article on that breakthrough yesterday!), and that already carries most of the implications for number theory that a full proof of RH would have. So who the hell knows what else is possible, and how quickly?

For those tuning in from home, the Riemann Hypothesis says (in its easiest-to-understand version) that the number of prime numbers from 1 to n is very close to what it would be if each integer x>1 had an independent 1/ln(x) probability of being prime, up to a standard statistical error term that never exceeds Õ(√n). While we’ve known since 1896 that the number of primes from 1 to n is asymptotic to n/ln(n) (that’s the famous Prime Number Theorem), you could’ve imagined the deviations being much larger.

David Hilbert famously said, “If I were to awaken after having slept for a thousand years, my first question would be: Has the Riemann Hypothesis been proven?” Meanwhile G. H. Hardy, on a ship that he feared might sink, sent his colleagues a telegram claiming to have proven RH, so that if the worst came to pass, at least the world might believe that a proof sank with him.

Many will of course question whether the proof announced today will stand. They’ll point out that, despite how heavily the world is now “lean-ing” on it, the Lean formal verification system still has issues, from kernel bugs (which have, in the past, allowed proofs of 0=1) to uncertain soundness of the underlying type theory. In my view, these issues can and should urgently be fixed! Until they are, a sufficiently motivated AI could almost certainly exploit them to prove a false statement!

All the same, I see zero indications that that’s happening right now. I note that, so far, not one of the AI results with Lean certificates has needed to be retracted (while several without Lean certificates have needed to be). So I’m not 100% sure, but my bet is that the proof will stand.

Mathematicians of course won’t be satisfied with 17 million lines of Lean.  They’ll be satisfied when, and only when, they’re able to explain and distill and reconstruct the ideas for themselves.  And that will probably take years, since human mathematicians move only at biological speeds.  And while they’re working on it, how many more such wonders will there be, in this age of wonders and terrors?

My 9-year-old son, informed that RH was proved, replied that he’s not even surprised at this point. Maybe you need to have come of age in the human math era to be surprised by such things.

The P=?NP problem now moves firmly into place as the Final Boss of the Math We’ve Cared About, the position I always thought it should occupy. But for how much longer? For how much longer will anything last that we currently take for granted?

It was only a couple days ago that my wife and I had the following conversation:

Dana: I turned off the irrigation, yet somehow water in our house is still leaking. We need to…

Me: Look, a lot of the smartest people I know now think that recursive self-improvement and the end of the entire known world are coming in 12-18 months. This leak…

Dana: We should still fix the leak.

item.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them (315 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://manidoraisamy.com/developer-to-architect.html, See on Hacker News


Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements:

  1. First, try to get the email if the user gave consent to share it during installation.
  2. If it fails, it would try to fetch his user ID.
  3. If that fails, it would log an error saying the user has installed, but we don’t know his email or user ID.

All of these are one line of code, but internally each of these makes multiple API calls to Google servers. Since logging was the first line to execute after installation, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load.

What is the right code for this?

If you are a senior developer or architect who understands the number of API calls behind each method, you would have:

  1. Logged just the timestamp of the install instead of trying to fetch the email or user ID, and told the marketing team they won’t be able to send the follow-up email based on installation alone.
  2. Or, if marketing wants the user’s email on install, you would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or user ID asynchronously from the browser, while the user is looking at the welcome screen. But calling your server from the addon’s welcome screen might require your server to bypass security and log an unauthenticated payload.

In other words, your job as an architect is to push back on requirements that can slow down the app. Or, find a way to work around the performance and security issues by making it async or accepting a reasonable hack.

Why AI won’t push back

AI is great at writing code. But it doesn’t know if you are launching the app or have millions of users, which it needs to make the right architecture call to log a timestamp vs email. It is also sycophantic and tries to execute your requirements exactly without pushing back, which means you end up with a slow app that takes 15 seconds to load a static welcome screen.

Essentially, if you generate code by specifying your requirements instead of specifying your architecture, AI will decide the architecture on your behalf. It is so paranoid about security that it will never write code to accept an unauthenticated payload. Even if you write it yourself, it will rewrite it into an authenticated payload and screw up performance or force users to sign in again on your app.

Your new job is to architect

AI coding tools are tuned to implement your functional requirements and two non-functional requirements, i.e. security and backward compatibility to avoid breaking your app. This invariably leads to:

  1. Architecture that trades off performance for security and slows down the app.
  2. Multiple versions of datamodel design with redundant tables, columns and code.

That means you define the architecture, design the datamodel first and ask AI to code within that constraint. Every time you give a requirement that changes your architecture or design, coding tools have to ask you before changing it, instead of changing it on their own. You have to tell it when it needs to be backward compatible, so it’s ok to keep multiple versions of logic or database tables, and when to delete the old logic and tables and keep a single version for maintainability.

If you are an architect who is used to designing the datamodel, delegating the implementation to developers and then reviewing their code to see if they have implemented it correctly, this should be natural to you. But the problem is that today we have taken developers who were great at coding and moved them into an architect’s job. They see that the job they love, i.e. coding, is now completely done by AI. But nobody has told them about the new job of pushing back on requirements, designing the datamodel, constraining AI to their architecture and reviewing that it falls in line. This is the reason for all the confusion and hate among developers about vibe coding.


Your future as developer

In our case, the right fix is simple. Log the timestamp, show the welcome screen first and tell marketing what they can’t get on install. But AI will never make that call for you, because it doesn’t know your users and it won’t push back on your requirements. That is the architect’s job. If you are a developer, the coding job is going away. But it doesn’t mean your job is going away. Non-developers who don’t understand architecture and design will end up with bad performance and unmaintainable database tables. So, stop missing the coding and become an architect. Learn to push back on requirements, design the datamodel, constrain AI to it and review the code the way an architect reviews a developer’s code. You got promoted. Nobody told you, so I am telling you.

item.title: Vibecoding an inference chip (117 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://ankitg.me/blog/vibecoding-inference-chip/, See on Hacker News

Or rather, I vibe-coded an FPGA into running an LLM. And it… just worked.

Friday. November 20, 2026

One of the more entertaining things about programming recently is that coding agents let me work in entirely new domains by giving me access to new programming languages and paradigms. Lately, that has meant hacking on hardware, now that writing low-level software is much easier. So, in this blog post, I’m going to try to recount the experience of vibe coding an FPGA, going through a series of “oh shit” moments several times, and giving myself a new appreciation for what’s possible if you have a large token budget (thanks YC) and interesting problems to point the models at.

I overheard some founders recently talk about how FPGAs work. I’ll admit I was relatively naive about them. I’d never really experimented with them in my startup or in college, so I knew little about them before. The basic idea I was familiar with: you can program a circuit into a reprogrammable chip. So rather than having a general purpose computing architecture (like a CPU) you can have a reprogrammable one, i.e. the configuration loaded onto the chip determines how its logic and routing are connected, and that (in theory) enables performance advantages. I also know that it took a mountain of C++ to write and involved manually analyzing waveforms for simulation and verification. I had never done this before though and it seemed cumbersome.

That’s about what I knew going into this.

Naturally, my ML brain thought “could we use these for AI inference”. I’m not the first to think this — there are a few repos attempting to port ML models to FPGAs on Github. But I hadn’t actually seen a writeup on whether coding agents are good at writing the low level C++ and Verilog code to program them and verifying the outputs so that they actually run accurately. (Spoiler alert, they are incredible at programming them.)

So I decided I needed to get my hands on one. AWS has F2 instances with FPGA hardware, and that seemed easier than going and buying physical hardware, so I asked Codex to spin up a reservation and got cooking. It had a relatively limited memory of 16 GB of FPGA HBM. Around the same time, I was working with the DeepGrove founders who were discussing their new ternary weight architecture that is well suited for memory limited cases. It’s SOTA on Mac hardware with actual agentic tool calling, so I figured why not, let’s see if I can get this working on an FPGA and fast enough to be useful.

What followed was a cloud agent running in Conductor for several days with me mostly just encouraging it periodically while it both (1) got a model fully running and (2) increased its speed by 33× from the first full-model bit-exact baseline to get it to a real-time relevant speed. It was one of the most mind blowing autoresearch loops I’ve run, ultimately writing roughly 3M lines across the experiment history and parsing 30M lines of output files, burning only $10,000 in Claude and OpenAI tokens to run hundreds of experiments. Most of the code is C++ and some Verilog. It’s been probably a decade since the last time I wrote any serious amount of C++ and I’ve never written Verilog. I honestly don’t know the first thing about Verilog. Most of my prompts were not particularly clever: they consisted mostly of me saying things like “you’re a superintelligent model, time to be more creative” and “let’s go for 2x faster, you got this”. Sometimes I brought some ML knowhow like “hey it’s time to consider speculative decoding” or “why is that running on CPU, you should port it”. But for the most part, it was just vibes and I’m pretty sure that with enough time the model would have figured out those things. Also, it seemed that both Astra and Opus (new Fable wasn’t out yet) were pretty capable at this and I could use them interchangeably. I’m sure someone has a good benchmark for which is smarter but both passed my smart-enough threshold.

From “it works” to 213 tokens per second

The chart follows the measured optimization sequence: 6 → 213 tokens/s, or 33× the baseline.

How much did the human advice help?

At one point, around when it got to 10 TPS, I messaged the DeepGrove founders about this, and they replied surprised that it was working so easily, saying they had tried this a few months back and the models were not quite good enough to be particularly effective. They sent me a prompt that summarizes some of their lessons and I copy-pasted it into my session to see if it’d matter. It was essentially the most significant piece of actual guidance I added to this session. The prompt is reproduced below.

Read the full FPGA design prompt

here is what someone else did for a dense bs=1 decode optimized fpga implementation for a dense qwen style model with ternary weights. you should take this with a grain of salt and pick things that you believe are acutally useful to add to your plan. Please also dont do things if you dont think is useful that take a lot of times like runnning really long test of a cycle accurate simulation etc or like physical design since those can take like hours. here are some ideas please pick and choose use this as context and not somehting that you shoudl be strictly guided by somethings that could help. prioritiize speed of like getting this up and running though..

MATMUL (TERNARY ENGINE)

  • No multipliers. A 2-bit weight drives a 3:1 mux that picks x, ~x, or 0. The unused 4th code raises an error flag, so corrupt weights get caught.
  • Negation is ~x + 1. Lanes flag negatives, and the row reducer adds the +1s once per row instead of once per lane.
  • Activations are grouped integers: INT12, or INT16 where we needed more range (MLP down projection). Reduce as integers, apply FP32 group scales, accumulate in FP32.
  • The pre-projection RMSNorm is deferred: quantize the activation first, apply the normalization scale after accumulation. It’s cheaper and numerically equivalent.
  • 8 cores in two clusters. Projections that are independent (gate/up) run at the same time on separate core groups.
  • Result: about half the DSPs of an INT8/INT16 design at the same rate, traded for more LUTs.

MEMORY

  • Weights are packed at 2 bits, 8x more per transfer than 16-bit. At batch 1, weight fetch costs far more energy and time than the math.
  • Weights stream from HBM straight into the compute lanes and skip the on-chip buffers (they’re used once per token). Activations are cached next to each core and reused across rows.
  • HBM routing is one chain per memory channel instead of a big crossbar. Lay out data so all 32 channels stay busy.
  • On-chip buffers are typed slots with an explicit lifecycle (open -> write -> commit -> read -> release). Each slot has a side memory for scales/exponents. The buffer checks format, range and producer, which catches scheduling bugs in hardware.
  • The KV cache is MXINT8: 8-bit values with one shared exponent per 32-channel block. That’s small enough to stream, with accuracy held.
  • For MoE: stripe each expert across every channel, and map expert ID to address at runtime instead of using a fixed program.

ATTENTION

  • Attention streams over the cache in 64-token tiles with an online softmax (FP32 running max/sum). The full score matrix is never stored.
  • Probabilities are UINT16 and the context accumulates in FP32.
  • Each attention unit interleaves two independent jobs on one datapath (C-slow), which hides pipeline latency without duplicating hardware.
  • Q/K head norm and RoPE got their own small vector unit, so they don’t block the general vector path. The V projection overlaps with that work.
  • New K/V is appended to HBM as soon as it’s produced. We used a sliding window to bound cache reads.

SCHEDULING

  • One controller issues work in program order, with tags and barriers. Engines overlap only when the buffer dependencies are explicit, so we got overlap without races.
  • For MoE: the router is the new critical path, because nothing can fetch until it finishes. Keep it in FP32 (lower precision changed which experts were picked), and overlap whatever you can around it.

CORRECTNESS (maybe not neecessary to folow super close)

  • We fixed a numerics contract first (formats, rounding points, operation order) and built hardware to match it. Vector ops must match the reference model’s order and precision, not just be “close”.
  • Verification ladder:
    1. Per-block cocotb unit tests.
    2. One full layer co-simulated against the real checkpoint.
    3. Multi-token, full 24-layer decode compared token-for-token with a reference oracle.
    4. Byte-level accounting of KV cache writes.
  • We kept simulation results, timing signoff and board results separate, and never claimed one from another.
  • Every published number links to the report it came from.

PHYSICAL DESIGN (maybe not necessary for u)

  • The chip has 3 regions (SLRs). Keep wide datapaths inside one region and register every crossing. Long links use credits, not combinational ready.
  • We placed engines next to their data: memory logic near HBM, attention in the DSP-dense region.
  • Screen logic depth (10 levels max at 250 MHz) right after synthesis, and fix it with pipelining, sharding, or C-slow. Full place-and-route is saved for integration.
  • Dev loop: small change -> lint -> unit test -> quick synthesis -> depth/timing check -> restructure.

The coding agent diligently considered these asks, but it didn’t seem to make all that much of a difference qualitatively. Indeed, when I asked it later to read all of the logs and determine which of these instructions it actually used, it said:

Read the agent’s retrospective: what it adopted and rejected

Its biggest design ideas were already in my plan before you pasted it. You pasted it on Oct 29 at 21:50 UTC: 4,741 characters describing what someone else did for a dense, batch-1, ternary FPGA decoder. Within 70 seconds I had sorted it into ten ideas to adopt and five to reject, and written that into every design agent’s brief. The shorter remark from your friend Edward, about using lookup tables as logic gates, came 24 minutes earlier and left nothing on the speed line.

Design ideas I adopted: mostly confirmation.

  • Already planned: streaming weights straight into the compute lanes, running rows in parallel, and reading the attention cache in bursts were all in the design brief I’d launched 35–40 minutes earlier.

  • Match what was later built:
    • interleaved lanes in the router (step 3);
    • a separate unit for head norms and RoPE (step 4);
    • a program-order sequencer (step 5);
    • a registered boundary on every crossing between dies (steps 8 and 12).
  • I can’t show these wouldn’t have happened without the notes.

Ideas I rejected: all five numerics shortcuts. Lower-precision activations, a deferred norm, an 8-bit KV cache, online softmax and 16-bit probabilities each change the output bits. That is where their design got its efficiency, and your bit-exact rule ruled it out.

Process advice: this changed things right away.

  • What you asked: not to do things that take hours.

  • What I stopped: a simulation that had run for about 24 hours, and two 250 MHz builds.

  • What I switched to: a short loop of C tests, synthesis and a logic-depth check, with one place-and-route per integration.

  • Likely gain: it got hardware results sooner.

  • Possible cost, which I can’t prove: two hangs that only RTL simulation could show reached the board the next day, and the big integration lost 38 hours to them.

One real find it triggered. While checking their memory ideas, I found AWS’s own reference memory design, which reaches 426 GB/s across all 32 memory channels. The memory subsystem was built from it.

In other words, for most of the actual design ideas it is unclear but there is good reason to believe the model would have figured them out, especially because it came up with them many cycles later after several compaction cycles. But the process advice was useful immediately for getting to hardware results sooner and increasing iteration speed. In other words, the humans are still useful at defining how to iterate fast and what correctness looks like, and the agents are great to manage the exploration.

The optimization log

Here are the changes the autoresearch loop found. Interestingly, it’s mostly a series of modest improvements that compound 1.5x ish every time, rather than one or two giant ones.

0Baseline6.43 tok/s

Baseline: the first full-model bit-exact FPGA image (R8), served with host-side prefix caching.

1.0× from baseline

1Host overhead8.07 tok/s

Host software only: per-command overhead fell from ~10 ms to 0.9 ms (persistent register mapping, streaming reads, no per-command SDK calls or fsyncs).

1.25× this step · 1.25× from baseline

2Burst attention14.02 tok/s

A 128-lane attention engine that reads the KV cache in bursts instead of a word at a time, keeping the reference's exact summation order.

1.74× this step · 2.18× from baseline

3Parallel router20.53 tok/s

A parallel MoE router with an exact GCC-sort tie-breaker plus a streaming output head with built-in argmax; moderate-effort routing let it run at 250 MHz.

1.46× this step · 3.19× from baseline

4Glue engine30.24 tok/s

A glue engine that parallelizes norms, RoPE, quantization and copies between engines in certified exact orders.

1.47× this step · 4.70× from baseline

5New pipeline49.21 tok/s

The full new pipeline (streaming ternary projection lanes + a new sequencer replacing R8's control path), after fixing two hangs that only appeared in hardware.

1.63× this step · 7.65× from baseline

6Prompt speculation51.25 tok/s

Exact speculative decoding: the host drafts tokens by prompt lookup and the FPGA verifies several in one pass.

1.04× this step · 7.97× from baseline

7Router relay58.43 tok/s

Fixed a relay that moved router weights between dies at 1/6 speed: router stall per layer 43,862 → 12,292 cycles.

1.14× this step · 9.08× from baseline

8Head shadow94.44 tok/s

Head shadow v2 (start the next token on a provisional guess; catch misses early) plus cross-die timing fixes, enabling 237.5 MHz kernel / 450 MHz memory.

1.62× this step · 14.68× from baseline

9Draft model105.63 tok/s

Exact speculative decoding with a real draft model: a cut-down Maple on the F2's host CPUs drafts ahead, and the FPGA verifies every token.

1.12× this step · 16.42× from baseline

10Memory ports108.81 tok/s

Doubled the memory ports from 4 to 8 (two projection lanes, output head striped across banks): 1.39× per clock, but congestion cut the clock to 181/375 MHz.

1.03× this step · 16.91× from baseline

11Attention overlap134.99 tok/s

Hid the attention engine's KV fetches behind its compute, and replaced the router's 2,048-step serial sum with an exact order-independent one (12,292 → 2,338 cycles per layer).

1.24× this step · 20.98× from baseline

12Weight packing171.3 tok/s

Lossless 5-trit weight packing (−20% weight bytes), shorter serial steps, and moving the output head to the far die, which relieved congestion and allowed 225/400 MHz.

1.27× this step · 26.63× from baseline

13Re-speculation184.19 tok/s

Re-speculation after head-shadow misses, speculative MoE expert prefill during the router, and a die rebalance (without the unused DDR controller) that ran 231.25/450 MHz on both boots.

1.08× this step · 28.63× from baseline

14Parallel head loader213.13 tok/s

A head loader that reads both of its memory banks at once (+17.3%, measured on and off on one image), a runtime expert-prefetch policy, and the router-job timing fix; run one clock step lower (225/425 MHz) after a soak test found random faults at 231.25.

1.16× this step · 33.13× from baseline

How it compares

It’s difficult to do a 1:1 comparison across these configurations. I didn’t run the same autoresearch loop on every alternative, and I assume there is more performance to extract if I did. The point is to show how slow the FPGA was in its first implementation, and how far the optimization loop took it.

The measurements below are from November 15 on AWS, replaying the same 8-chat × 3-turn benchmark. Prices are the on-demand rates recorded with that experiment. “Exact turns” counts outputs that matched the pinned CPU reference. The GPU implementations are included for context but did not satisfy the same bit-exact criterion but are pretty close in practice.

What happens as the context grows?

This is one generation starting with a 16-token prompt and continuing until the 8,192-token context is full: 8,176 generated tokens. The five middle columns show decode speed in tokens/s at the indicated context length for several generations of iteration. The last column is wall-clock time for the whole run/

* For r8 and r9, the first two columns come from separate, shorter runs generating 2,032 tokens. The other columns come from the full-context run.

r9 improves short-context speed, while the complete long-context run is roughly tied with r8.

What the model actually says

These examples come from the final r9 image.

Arithmetic, with the steps

246 tokens · 229.7 tokens/s · 1.16 s end to end

Read the arithmetic transcript 
USER: What is 37 × 48? Explain the steps briefly.

MODEL: <think>
We need to compute 37 × 48. The user asks to explain steps briefly. So I'll do multiplication: 37 × 48 = 37 × (50 - 2) = 37×50 - 37×2 = 1850 - 74 = 1776. Or directly: 37×40=1480, 37×8=296, sum=1776. I'll present a brief explanation.
</think>

To multiply 37 by 48, you can break it down:

- 37 × 48 = 37 × (50 – 2) = (37 × 50) – (37 × 2) = 1850 – 74 = 1776.

Alternatively, 37 × 40 = 1480 and 37 × 8 = 296, so 1480 + 296 = 1776.

The final answer is **1776**.

A little Python

140 tokens · 220.0 tokens/s · 0.76 s end to end

System prompt: “You are a helpful assistant. Think briefly before you answer, then reply clearly and concisely.”

Read the Python transcript 
USER: Write a Python function is_palindrome(s) that ignores case, spaces and punctuation.

MODEL: <think>
We need to write a Python function is_palindrome(s) that ignores case, spaces, and punctuation. So we need to filter out non-alphanumeric characters, convert to lowercase, then check if the resulting string is equal to its reverse. Provide the code.
</think>

```python
def is_palindrome(s: str) -> bool:
    """
    Returns True if the string s is a palindrome, ignoring case, spaces, and punctuation.
    """
    # Filter to keep only alphanumeric characters and convert to lowercase
    filtered = ''.join(ch.lower() for ch in s if ch.isalnum())
    # Compare with its reverse
    return filtered == filtered[::-1]
```

Where this puts us

This was a fun project. I’m not sure I’m ever going to use this specific chip architecture in this specific way, and I’m certainly not claiming that an 8,192-token-context model running on an FPGA is the way I’d recommend anyone use something like this in production. But it’s pretty epic that this just works. Capability like this completely shifts the overton window for what a committed team of engineers can work on. It should mean that entirely new types of ideas (scientific discoveries, products, startups) are possible if you can point the models in the right direction. I’m excited to see what everyone builds.

item.title: Anthropic shares tank after IPO as the Nasdaq erases 2026 gains (183 pts)

A bruising stock market sell-off gathered steam Friday, despite high hopes that Anthropic’s record-setting IPO a day earlier would revive sentiment around the flagging AI trade.

Instead, Friday’s downturn was led by Anthropic itself, whose shares were down more than 11% after rising 17% on its first day on the Nasdaq Composite.

The S&P 500 was trading nearly 2% lower as it headed for its worst losing week since April 2025, when President Donald Trump announced his “Liberation Day” tariffs, and is now 10% off from its most recent high, entering what’s known as “correction territory.”

Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was off more than 3% and officially erasing all its previous gains in 2026. Other major AI-related names such as CoreWeave, Nvidia and Oracle also sold off.

The six consecutive declining S&P 500 sessions mark the index’s longest losing streak since April 2024. A seventh losing day would make it the longest stretch since the pandemic slump in February 2020, according to Deutsche Bank.

For U.S. households relying on 401(k)s and pension funds for retirement, the downturn is especially unwelcome at a time when inflation continues to prove stubborn.

Given the importance the AI trade has played this year in propelling markets and economic growth writ large, its derailment over concerns about costs, debt, profitability and political risk could have broader implications.

Deepening worries about AI revenues tied to exports of advanced technology to China compounded Friday’s sell-off.

The Jensen Huang scandal pulling down Nvidia appeared to broaden Thursday, when a short-selling firm issued a report raising questions about whether Advanced Micro Devices, another chip giant, may also have had shipments to Asia diverted to mainland China.

Alongside the stock sell-off, there has been an increase in purchases of U.S. Treasury bonds — a sign that investors are seeing signs of weakening growth amid higher interest rates from the Federal Reserve and a stalling economy in China.

“The pressure is becoming increasingly widespread, and that’s been felt across other asset classes too,” Deutsche Bank managing director Jim Reid wrote in a note to clients Friday.

Kevin Gordon, head of macroeconomic strategy and research at Charles Schwab, told NBC News that markets are feeling particular pressure from an increasingly “hawkish” Federal Reserve that is signaling aggressive rate hikes in the face of unrelenting inflation.

Obviously these results will be reported widely in other outlets, but I will note them here, in decreasing order of how “digested” the results currently are:

  • Levent Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster, and Matei Coiculescu, with heavy AI assistance, have written a human-readable proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Euler equations in three dimensions, which is formalized in Lean here.
  • Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster, again with heavy AI usage, have generated a proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Navier Stokes equations in three dimensions, again with a Lean formalization. Here, the paper is technically human-readable and the general strategy of proof is broadly clear (following one of the expected paths to this result, namely to numerically build an approximate discretely self-similar solution and then use rigorous perturbation theory to convert this to an exact solution); but more work needs to be done to create a proper, professionally written proof.
  • Levent Alpöge, using an internal AI model, has generated an (enormous) Lean-only proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. This Lean Zulip thread is probably the best place to follow the efforts to verify the proof and extract the strategy of proof (which, from very initial analysis, appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry). (UPDATE: the moderators of the Lean thread are now focusing the discussion on the Lean-related aspects of the proof only.) I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task.

See also Buckmaster’s Mastodon post regarding the first two results.

As I wrote last week after attending a rally in New York City:

Attendees of all ages held signs reading, “NO AI IN MY SCHOOL!”, “A.I. Gets an F,” “Stop stealing our imaginations,” and “SCHOOL Librarians = THE BEST Search Engines.” Some students handed out fliers to passersby while younger children ran around and drew pictures off to the side.

That day, protests took place in six other cities—Los Angeles; Chicago; Boston; Portland, Oregon; Boulder, Colorado; and Durham, North Carolina—all organized by a nationwide alliance of parent and community advocacy organizations.

School districts across the country use the company’s software and Chromebooks, which were more affordable than Windows and Apple computers when many were quickly assembling remote learning programs during the early years of the Covid pandemic. The Chromebooks have built-in AI classroom tools, and Google Search embeds AI Overview and AI Mode powered by Gemini. 

Responding to the backlash, three of the largest school districts in the US—New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago—are now discussing alternative search engines. 

“Any opportunity to drive positive change with AI in education will rely on educators having the freedom to choose how to implement it in their curriculum,” employees wrote in a petition brought by the Alphabet Workers Union, which represents more than 1,000 workers at Google’s parent company. “Cutting off access to Search for schools that don’t wish to use AI will not help persuade our users, and will more likely result in them shutting out Google products altogether.”

Another engineer and union member in New York, who also signed the petition, said to Mother Jones that the executive team “seems convinced that resistance to AI adoption is because people don’t see the vision.”

That goes beyond teachers, parents, and students: the Google staffer said their colleagues are also concerned about how the company is implementing their work on AI tools.

item.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights (344 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21885, See on Hacker News

Authors:Jiajun Fan, Neil He, Changyi Yang, Andy Mao, Xi Zhu, Chaoran Cheng, Kaiqu Liang, Shuaike Shen, Zetian Li, Ruihan Guo, Ge Liu

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract:A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.
